summary: RFC 8226 provides a certificate extension to constrain the JWT claims allowed in a PASSporT, and the recipient rejects the whole PASSporT if a claim falls outside the constraints. This document updates RFC 8226 with an enhanced extension that keeps the original capabilities and adds another way to constrain allowable claims.

eli5.summary: A phone-call ID card can say which details the caller may put on it. This document adds a new way to write those limits.

questions: what is the enhanced jwt claim constraints extension
what is mustexclude in a stir certificate
how do stir certificates limit passport claims
subtitle: A certificate extension that lets a STIR certificate say which claims a signed call token must carry, may carry, or must never carry.

tldr.problem: RFC 8226 lets a STIR certificate require certain JWT claims in a PASSporT or limit their values, but it cannot say that a claim must be absent. That matters when a service provider hands signing authority to a customer.
tldr.mechanism: The Enhanced JWT Claim Constraints extension keeps the old mustInclude and permittedValues lists and adds mustExclude, a list of claims that must not appear. A recipient treats a PASSporT that breaks any list as invalid.
tldr.outcome: Certificate issuers can now forbid specific claims, but the extension is non-critical, so only relying parties that recognize it will enforce it. The RFC updates RFC 8226.

today: RFC 9118 is a Proposed Standard from August 2021 that updates RFC 8226, and nothing in the metadata marks it as obsoleted or updated. The RFC itself notes that until the enhanced extension is widely implemented, the original extension may be more likely to be supported.

sections.title: Why the Extension Exists
sections.content:
STIR certificates, described in RFC 8226, help prevent the impersonation of telephone numbers on the Internet. Section 8 of RFC 8226 gives them an extension that constrains the JSON Web Token (JWT) claims allowed in a Personal Assertion Token (PASSporT), which is defined in RFC 8225. If a signer includes a claim outside the constraints, the recipient rejects the entire PASSporT.

The original extension can list claims that must be included and the permitted values for chosen claims. RFC 9118 defines an enhanced extension that does all of that and adds a list of claims that must not be included.

The need comes from delegation. When a parent STIR certificate hands authority to a subordinate certificate, the parent wants to limit what the subordinate can sign. RFC 9060 describes service providers issuing STIR certificates to enterprises or other customers, and the new extension can keep specific claims out of PASSporTs that recipients would accept.
sections.eli5: Imagine a school lets a club print membership cards. It can already say which boxes must be filled in. Now it can also say which boxes must stay empty.

sections.title: The Three Constraint Lists
sections.content:
The Enhanced JWT Claim Constraints extension is non-critical, applies only to end-entity certificates, and is written in ASN.1. It is optional, but when present it limits the claims an authentication service may put in the PASSporTs it signs. Issuers set the constraints and recipients enforce them. It is identified by id-pe-eJWTClaimConstraints, which is { id-pe 33 }.

The extension holds up to three optional lists, and at least one of them must be present:

  • mustInclude: claims that MUST appear in the PASSporT in addition to iat, orig and dest. Those three baseline claims are already required by RFC 8225 and SHOULD NOT be listed. If mustInclude is absent, the three baseline claims still MUST appear.
  • permittedValues: if the named claim is present, its value MUST exactly match one of the listed values.
  • mustExclude: claims that MUST NOT appear. The baseline claims are always permitted and MUST NOT be listed. If one is listed, the certificate MUST be treated as if the extension were not present.

Claim names MUST be ASCII strings, following RFC 8226. They are encoded as IA5String, and permitted values as UTF8String.
sections.eli5: There are three lists on the card: things you must write, the only answers you may write in a box, and things you must never write.

sections.title: Usage Examples
sections.content:
The RFC uses an imaginary PASSporT claim called confidence with the values low, medium and high.

  • With confidence in mustInclude, the authentication service has to put the claim in every PASSporT it signs, and a verification service treats a PASSporT without it as invalid.
  • With confidence in permittedValues and only high allowed, a PASSporT carrying any other value is invalid. A PASSporT with no confidence claim at all is not invalid, unless confidence is also in mustInclude.
  • With confidence in mustExclude, any PASSporT carrying the claim is invalid, whatever its value.

The RFC also gives a full example certificate and decodes its extension. That extension imposes three constraints: confidence must be present, it must have the value high or medium, and the priority claim must not be present.
sections.eli5: If the rule says a box must be filled, an empty box is wrong. If it says only certain answers are allowed, other answers are wrong. If it says a box is banned, any answer in it is wrong.

sections.title: Guidance to Certification Authorities
sections.content:
The new EnhancedJWTClaimConstraints extension and the JWTClaimConstraints extension from RFC 8226 MUST NOT both appear in the same certificate.

If a situation needs mustExclude, only the enhanced extension can express it. If it does not, either extension will do. The RFC adds that until support for the enhanced extension is widely implemented, the older extension may be more likely to be supported. It describes this as a guess based on the presumption that the first specified extension will be implemented more widely in the next few years.
sections.eli5: A card gets one rulebook, not two. If you need the new ban rule, you must use the new rulebook. If not, the old one may be understood in more places.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because the extension is non-critical, implementations that do not recognize its object identifier ignore it. Constraints on PASSporT validation are applied only by relying parties that recognize it. Enforcement also depends on correct implementation by verification services, and the digital signature on the PASSporT stays valid even when the limits are violated.

Issuers must be careful with combinations. An entry in mustInclude and an entry in mustExclude for the same claim means no PASSporT can ever validate. Issuers SHOULD NOT put the rcdi claim in mustExclude for a certificate used with the PASSporT Extension for Rich Call Data, because excluding it would break that extension's integrity protection.

When a certificate is renewed, the new one must carry exactly the same extension as the old one. Old and new certificates are both valid for a while, and different constraints under the same public key could make some PASSporTs valid with one certificate and invalid with the other.
sections.eli5: A rule only works where people read it. And if a card both demands and bans the same box, no one can ever fill it in correctly.

sections.title: IANA Assignments and the ASN.1 Module
sections.content:
IANA assigned decimal value 33 to id-pe-eJWTClaimConstraints in the registry for PKIX certificate extensions (1.3.6.1.5.5.7.1). It also assigned 101 to the module identifier id-mod-eJWTClaimConstraints-2021 in the registry for PKIX module identifiers (1.3.6.1.5.5.7.0).

Appendix A holds the full ASN.1 module. It imports definitions from RFC 5912 and is compatible with the ASN.1 specifications published in 2015.
sections.eli5: The new rule got its own official number in the big list of numbers, so everyone can recognize it.
